A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FS-SINR research, despite the added 'Feedforward' in v2's title. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching extensively relocated supplementary content.

before.justification: V1 reports original IUCN and S&T evaluations, quantitative ablations, and qualitative range predictions, including Figure 3, Table 1, and Appendices B–D.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds ensemble uncertainty evaluations, traditional-method comparisons, timing measurements, and expanded context-budget results.

M1.justification: The core architecture, training losses, and single-model inference procedure remain unchanged. V2 Appendix A.1 adds a limited inference extension: averaging predictions from three FS-SINR models and using their prediction variance to estimate uncertainty. The DINOv2 variant already existed in v1.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same iNaturalist-derived training resources and IUCN/S&T evaluation datasets, with location, text, image, and taxonomic inputs. Non-species concept examples also already existed. The added 500- and 1,000-location evaluations change sample counts within retained tasks, not dataset or population coverage.

E2.justification: V2 Appendix A.5 and Figure A6 add evaluated Gaussian Process and Random Forest comparators on both benchmarks. This substantially broadens comparisons beyond the retained SINR, LE-SINR, Prototype SINR, and Active SINR methods to traditional machine-learning approaches.

E3.justification: V2 adds 500- and 1,000-context evaluations, an uncertainty protocol that removes the most uncertain 2% of locations iteratively, and CPU/GPU timing comparisons using one location plus text. The new traditional baselines use one pseudo-negative per context location. These expand evaluation design; retained training settings and benchmark protocols are otherwise largely unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds an analysis of whether ensemble disagreement predicts errors, extends DINOv2 testing beyond v1's zero-shot results, and examines behavior at much larger context budgets. Figures 5 and 6 add qualitative cases. Conversely, v1's location-embedding ICA analysis and training-density visualization are removed. Most original architectural, taxonomic, and ecological analyses are retained through relocation.

E5.justification: Both versions already report three-run means, standard-deviation bars, grouped-result standard errors, and qualitative seed variability. V2 adds predictive uncertainty estimation using ensemble variance, uncertainty maps, and SEAUC/AURG reporting in Appendix A.1 and Table A1. This is a substantial new uncertainty analysis, not evidence of an increased repeated-run count.

E6.justification: Shared values in Table 1, Tables A3–A4, and the relocated zero-shot and taxonomy tables remain unchanged. V2 adds traditional-baseline results, DINOv2 few-shot entries, and 500/1,000-context results. Table A1 reports S&T zero-shot ensemble MAP of 0.66 versus 0.64 for individual models. Section 4.2 newly reports runtime at 2% of LE-SINR's CPU time and 6% of its GPU time.

T1.justification: V2 Appendix A.1 introduces adapted mathematical definitions of MAP-based sparsification-curve area and AURG relative to a random/MAP baseline. Existing losses, prototype and Active SINR equations, and the distance-weighted MAP definition are retained with notation or numbering changes. No theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same contributions: feedforward prediction for unseen species without retraining, multimodal conditioning, and leading zero/few-shot performance. The conclusion's 5–10% improvement claim is unchanged. The revised title emphasizes an existing claim; added timing and comparison results provide supporting evidence.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations of image-induced bias and spurious features, interprets ensemble uncertainty, and connects poor small-range performance to conservation concerns. It also explains why S&T's partial geographic coverage prevents certain global analyses. Most geographic and taxonomic bias interpretations already appeared in v1; their increased prominence largely reflects relocation.

D1.justification: V2 replaces the promised future code release with an explicit repository availability statement, identifies evaluation text as generated summaries, and supplies implementation choices for the new Gaussian Process and Random Forest comparisons. It removes v1's instruction to skip examples when all modalities are dropped, without establishing an actual procedure change. Most architecture, hyperparameter, hardware, and training-time details remain unchanged.

R1.justification: V2 adds citations supporting traditional baselines, ensembles, uncertainty evaluation, sampling bias, and extinction risk: Breiman, Golding and Purse, Dietterich, Poggi, Hughes, and Chichorro. Positioning relative to SINR and LE-SINR remains stable. SATCLIP's preprint-to-publication update refers to the same work.

P1.justification: Besides widespread prose editing and the revised title, v2 substantially reorganizes the appendix. V1's implementation–ablations–qualitative–quantitative sequence becomes quantitative results–ecological analysis–implementation–ablations–qualitative results, with an overview and regrouped subsections. The experimental narrative also expands to explain and connect the supplementary findings.

P2.justification: V2 adds ensemble and traditional-baseline displays, expands Figures 5–6, and adds columns and rows to Tables A3–A4. It removes v1 Figures A17 and A24 and extensively relocates retained displays. Qualitative figures receive revised labels and expert-range insets, including correction of the American Pika text labels. These are substantial presentation changes despite many retained plot values.

improvement.justification: V2 strengthens validation through measured efficiency, traditional-baseline comparisons, ensemble uncertainty testing, and larger-context evaluations. Code access information and clearer appendix organization improve usability. These are useful extensions to an already extensive evaluation, while headline results and central limitations remain unchanged. Removing the embedding and training-density visualizations loses some diagnostic evidence, but the additions provide a limited net quality improvement.
